See how this bachelor compares with study options at UCR

This is a pre-produced programme comparison. Your search helped you find the programme; it did not personalize the comparison.

← Back to search

The English-taught International Bachelor History at Erasmus University Rotterdam studies global historical change and uses historical and social-science methods to investigate contemporary questions. Students choose a focus area and complete an individual History thesis.

The first UCR option combines historical inquiry with economic and social explanation. The second focuses on international relations, conflict and institutions; the third on social and cultural history. Each includes all six UCR History courses and a primary-source research seminar. Economics, law, rhetoric and other fields support those historical questions while retaining their own methods. Shared rows show partial subject or skill relationships; blank cells preserve substantive gaps.

Academic year: 2026–2027

External pathway: Economic History; minor and selected internship

One permitted 2026–2027 pathway is shown. Other focus areas and the approved elective, exchange and educational-minor routes remain available.

What this comparison shows

A curriculum-level comparison of International Bachelor History at Erasmus University Rotterdam with 3 illustrative UCR study compositions.

CLOSEST UCR MATCH
History, economy & society

Modern history, empire, warfare, gender and Indigenous histories form the core. Economics and sociology support analysis of economic and social change, while art history, historiography, qualitative and quantitative methods, primary-source research and rhetoric develop interpretation and communication.

ADDITIONAL UCR OPTION
History, international relations & conflict

Modern history, empires, Western warfare, gender and Indigenous histories are studied alongside international-relations theory, political thought, comparative politics, conflict and peace, human rights and legal institutions. Sociology, qualitative research and public rhetoric support historically informed analysis of power and international order.

ADDITIONAL UCR OPTION
Social & cultural history

Historical inquiry into societies and cultural expression combines all six History courses with sociology, social movements, art and material culture, archaeology, heritage, museums, literature, film, race and documentary. Historical and art-historical research, qualitative methods and public rhetoric support analysis of evidence, representation and memory.

Important limitation

This is a curriculum comparison. A UCR composition is not the same disciplinary degree and does not by itself establish a professional qualification or automatic eligibility for a particular master’s programme.

Rows show curricular relationships, including partial matches, rather than course equivalence. A blank cell means there is no closely comparable component in that row. Optional independent research is additional to the displayed 180 EC.

modals.text:
Personal & Professional Development
This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
Close

Introduction to Economics
Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.
Close

International Macroeconomics
Study the economy as a whole through topics such as national income, economic growth, inflation, and unemployment. Understand how governments and central banks use fiscal and monetary policies to influence economic performance over time. The course also explores business cycles, international trade, and economic crises, preparing students to evaluate policy debates and global economic trends.
Close

Microeconomics & Behavior
Study how consumers and producers make decisions under scarcity. Explore key concepts such as rational choice, decision-making under uncertainty, and non-egoistic preferences. Analyze market structures, strategic interactions, and factor markets. Learn how markets function and examine the impact of regulation. Develop analytical tools to better understand behavior and engage with empirical research.
Close

Public Economics
Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.
Close

Econometrics
Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.
Close

Research Methods & Statistics
Research Methods & Statistics introduces research design, operationalisation, sampling, experiments and surveys. Students study descriptive and inferential statistics, association, hypothesis testing and analysis of variance, with an introduction to multivariate applications. A group research project applies these methods to a chosen research problem.
Close

Law, Society & Justice
Law, Society & Justice examines legal, social and normative perspectives on law. Students explore legal systems and fields including constitutional, administrative, criminal and international law, human rights and selected private-law topics. Case law and trial simulations support discussion of law, society and justice.
Close

Modern History
Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.
Close

Histories of Gender
Studies gender, storytelling and marginalised lives in the nineteenth- to twenty-first-century American context. Students examine slavery, community activism, representation and lived experience, using sources and projects that connect historical interpretation with contemporary questions.
Close

History of Empires
History of Empires examines major empires and the contested meaning of empire. Students consider theories of imperial rise and decline, sources of imperial power and great-power politics, including competing claims about oppression and social improvement.
Close

Western Way of War
Provides a chronological overview of warfare in the Western world from antiquity to the present. Covers weapons, technology, strategy, defence, mercenaries, cavalry, chivalry, Blitzkrieg, guerrilla warfare and nuclear arsenals, illustrating competition for mastery in Western history.
Close

Native American Histories
Native American Histories studies Indigenous history and life from the nineteenth to the twenty-first century. Work with Indigenous students, scholars and elders addresses boarding schools, human trafficking, Traditional Ecological Knowledge, cultural resistance and regeneration. Indigenous methodologies emphasise storytelling, reciprocity and relational knowledge; gender studies, psychology and sociology help connect past and present.
Close

History Research Seminar
Investigates the 1809 Walcheren Expedition through primary sources, including diaries, letters, memoirs and official reports from different participants. Students learn to find, read and analyse historical evidence and write a substantial research paper, with considerable independent study.
Close

Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties.
Close

Introduction to Public International Law
Introduction to Public International Law examines the creation and historical development of international law, its sources, subjects and organisation. Topics include the use of force, armed conflict, international criminal law, refugees and environmental law, followed by self-determination, Third World Approaches and treaty politics. Assessment includes exercises, exams, a podcast and reflection.
Close

Comparative Constitutional Law
Comparative Constitutional Law studies constitutional and administrative law through comparison of five legal systems. Students examine how constitutions establish public institutions, define government powers and protect rights and liberties, alongside the relationship between law, democracy and the constitutional state.
Close

Foundations of European Union Law
Introduces the EU legal order. Studies institutions, framework, citizenship and the internal market using problem‑based exercises and guest lectures.
Close

Introduction to Political Philosophy
Introduction to Political Philosophy examines influential Western thinkers from classical antiquity to the present. Students study views of human nature, society and political authority, place theories in their historical settings and compare their arguments and proposed solutions with contemporary political problems.
Close

Foundations of Comparative Politics
Provides analytical tools to compare political systems and democracies. Examines phenomena like democratic backsliding, decline of political parties, rise of populism, media changes, non‑majoritarian institutions and globalization’s impact on domestic politics.
Close

Theory of International Relations
Theory of International Relations introduces schools of thought about international relations and geopolitics. Students apply theories to historical and contemporary cases through readings, group presentations, homework and an exam. A United Nations Security Council simulation asks students to represent a member state in a current international problem.
Close

European Union Politics
Introduces EU politics. Outlines actors, institutions and decision‑making rules; examines responses to crises; and employs various approaches to study EU politics and policy‑making.
Close

Peace & Conflict
Peace & Conflict introduces theories about the causes, consequences and possible resolution of violent and nonviolent conflicts. Historical and contemporary cases address structural inequality, ideology, humiliation and colonial or postcolonial grievances. Students compare international, institutional, cultural and civil-society perspectives and examine how concepts such as justice, truth and reconciliation travel between fields.
Close

Introduction to Sociology
Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
Close

Qualitative Research Methodology
Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
Close

Modern Sociology
Examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and colonial responses. Studies leading social theories and debates about modernity and critically engages with sociological discourses.
Close

Social Movements & Environmental Justice
Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement.
Close

New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
Examines contemporary sociological debates about civil society through critical tradition, neo‑functionalism and decolonial critiques. Includes research group projects with NGOs or civil society organizations that translate conceptual insights into empirical analysis.
Close

The Art of Rhetorical Communication
The Art of Rhetorical Communication develops rhetorical analysis, academic writing and oral presentation. Students examine classical Western roots and the canons of rhetoric, and learn to construct, organise and support persuasive arguments. Historical and contemporary examples connect rhetorical theory with practical communication.
Close

Rhetoric in Action
Develops persuasive speaking skills by applying rhetorical theory in the real world. Students work with local primary school children, building public-speaking skills and empowering them to find their voices.
Close

Introduction to Western Art History
Introduction to Western Art History surveys Western art from the early Renaissance to the present. Key paintings, artists and movements introduce visual analysis and interpretation. The course also considers how institutions, markets, critics and historiographers shape the understanding and legacy of artworks.
Close

Introduction to World Archaeology
Introduction to World Archaeology explores craft production and material culture in ancient societies around the world. Students examine how making objects relates to religious, social and gendered identities, technologies and environmental effects. An experimental educational activity and discussion of contemporary archaeological methods connect interpretation with practice.
Close

African Art & Heritage
Examines the artistic, historical and ethical dimensions of African art. Highlights distinct forms and cultural significance, considers influence on Western modernism and addresses looting, colonial-era acquisitions and repatriation efforts.
Close

Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean
This course examines the painting, sculpture, and architecture of Renaissance Italy and the extensive artistic connections that linked the Italian peninsula to other regions of the world. By exploring a range of geographical contexts, from the Islamic courts of the Eastern Mediterranean and the commercial routes connecting Europe, Asia, and Africa to the newly encountered territories of the Americas, students will examine how trade, colonization, and cross-cultural exchange shaped the production and meaning of Renaissance art.
Close

Modern Art & Modern Museums
Examines debates on modern art through various themes. Focuses on the relationship between art and its presentation in museums and exhibitions, exploring curatorial practices and exhibition strategies.
Close

Writing Art's Histories
This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.
Close

Introduction to Literary Studies
Introduction to Literary Studies introduces practical criticism and literary interpretation. Students examine what literature is, why it is read and studied, formal properties and the constructed character of texts. Fiction, poetry and drama are supplemented by contemporary nonfiction and basic film narration, developing critical terms, tools and techniques.
Close

Film & Text
Studies complex links between literary and film narratives. Analyzes formal aspects of both media, discusses adaptation, intertextuality, viewer participation and narrative dynamics, and allows students to research topics like literature‑to‑film adaptation and cross‑cultural themes.
Close

Media & Race
Media & Race investigates storytelling, power, privilege, resistance and systemic racism in American history from the late nineteenth century to the present. Film, photographs, music and other media connect past and present. Students produce research-based podcasts exploring how media sustains oppression and supports resistance.
Close

The Documentary
Introduces documentary film from its early development to contemporary forms, analysing historical and social contexts, styles and genres, and ethical and aesthetic questions. Students analyse non-fiction representations and produce a short documentary item.
Close

International Macroeconomics

Understand how governments and central banks use fiscal and monetary policies to influence economic performance over time. The course also explores business cycles, international trade, and economic crises, preparing students to evaluate policy debates and global economic trends.
Close

Microeconomics & Behavior
Study how consumers and producers make decisions under scarcity. Explore key concepts such as rational choice, decision-making under uncertainty, and non-egoistic preferences. Analyze market structures, strategic interactions, and factor markets. Learn how markets function and examine the impact of regulation. Develop analytical tools to better understand behavior and engage with empirical research.
Close

Public Economics
Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.
Close

Econometrics
Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.
Close

Research Methods & Statistics
Research Methods & Statistics introduces research design, operationalisation, sampling, experiments and surveys. Students study descriptive and inferential statistics, association, hypothesis testing and analysis of variance, with an introduction to multivariate applications. A group research project applies these methods to a chosen research problem.
Close

Law, Society & Justice
Law, Society & Justice examines legal, social and normative perspectives on law. Students explore legal systems and fields including constitutional, administrative, criminal and international law, human rights and selected private-law topics. Case law and trial simulations support discussion of law, society and justice.
Close

Modern History
Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.
Close

Histories of Gender
Studies gender, storytelling and marginalised lives in the nineteenth- to twenty-first-century American context. Students examine slavery, community activism, representation and lived experience, using sources and projects that connect historical interpretation with contemporary questions.
Close

History of Empires
History of Empires examines major empires and the contested meaning of empire. Students consider theories of imperial rise and decline, sources of imperial power and great-power politics, including competing claims about oppression and social improvement.
Close

Western Way of War
Provides a chronological overview of warfare in the Western world from antiquity to the present. Covers weapons, technology, strategy, defence, mercenaries, cavalry, chivalry, Blitzkrieg, guerrilla warfare and nuclear arsenals, illustrating competition for mastery in Western history.
Close

Native American Histories
Native American Histories studies Indigenous history and life from the nineteenth to the twenty-first century. Work with Indigenous students, scholars and elders addresses boarding schools, human trafficking, Traditional Ecological Knowledge, cultural resistance and regeneration. Indigenous methodologies emphasise storytelling, reciprocity and relational knowledge; gender studies, psychology and sociology help connect past and present.
Close

History Research Seminar
Investigates the 1809 Walcheren Expedition through primary sources, including diaries, letters, memoirs and official reports from different participants. Students learn to find, read and analyse historical evidence and write a substantial research paper, with considerable independent study.
Close

Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties.
Close

Introduction to Public International Law
Introduction to Public International Law examines the creation and historical development of international law, its sources, subjects and organisation. Topics include the use of force, armed conflict, international criminal law, refugees and environmental law, followed by self-determination, Third World Approaches and treaty politics. Assessment includes exercises, exams, a podcast and reflection.
Close

Comparative Constitutional Law
Comparative Constitutional Law studies constitutional and administrative law through comparison of five legal systems. Students examine how constitutions establish public institutions, define government powers and protect rights and liberties, alongside the relationship between law, democracy and the constitutional state.
Close

Foundations of European Union Law
Introduces the EU legal order. Studies institutions, framework, citizenship and the internal market using problem‑based exercises and guest lectures.
Close

Introduction to Political Philosophy
Introduction to Political Philosophy examines influential Western thinkers from classical antiquity to the present. Students study views of human nature, society and political authority, place theories in their historical settings and compare their arguments and proposed solutions with contemporary political problems.
Close

Foundations of Comparative Politics
Provides analytical tools to compare political systems and democracies. Examines phenomena like democratic backsliding, decline of political parties, rise of populism, media changes, non‑majoritarian institutions and globalization’s impact on domestic politics.
Close

Theory of International Relations
Theory of International Relations introduces schools of thought about international relations and geopolitics. Students apply theories to historical and contemporary cases through readings, group presentations, homework and an exam. A United Nations Security Council simulation asks students to represent a member state in a current international problem.
Close

European Union Politics
Introduces EU politics. Outlines actors, institutions and decision‑making rules; examines responses to crises; and employs various approaches to study EU politics and policy‑making.
Close

Peace & Conflict
Peace & Conflict introduces theories about the causes, consequences and possible resolution of violent and nonviolent conflicts. Historical and contemporary cases address structural inequality, ideology, humiliation and colonial or postcolonial grievances. Students compare international, institutional, cultural and civil-society perspectives and examine how concepts such as justice, truth and reconciliation travel between fields.
Close

Introduction to Sociology
Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
Close

Qualitative Research Methodology
Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
Close

Modern Sociology
Examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and colonial responses. Studies leading social theories and debates about modernity and critically engages with sociological discourses.
Close

Social Movements & Environmental Justice
Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement.
Close

New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
Examines contemporary sociological debates about civil society through critical tradition, neo‑functionalism and decolonial critiques. Includes research group projects with NGOs or civil society organizations that translate conceptual insights into empirical analysis.
Close

The Art of Rhetorical Communication
The Art of Rhetorical Communication develops rhetorical analysis, academic writing and oral presentation. Students examine classical Western roots and the canons of rhetoric, and learn to construct, organise and support persuasive arguments. Historical and contemporary examples connect rhetorical theory with practical communication.
Close

Rhetoric in Action
Develops persuasive speaking skills by applying rhetorical theory in the real world. Students work with local primary school children, building public-speaking skills and empowering them to find their voices.
Close

Introduction to Western Art History
Introduction to Western Art History surveys Western art from the early Renaissance to the present. Key paintings, artists and movements introduce visual analysis and interpretation. The course also considers how institutions, markets, critics and historiographers shape the understanding and legacy of artworks.
Close

Introduction to World Archaeology
Introduction to World Archaeology explores craft production and material culture in ancient societies around the world. Students examine how making objects relates to religious, social and gendered identities, technologies and environmental effects. An experimental educational activity and discussion of contemporary archaeological methods connect interpretation with practice.
Close

African Art & Heritage
Examines the artistic, historical and ethical dimensions of African art. Highlights distinct forms and cultural significance, considers influence on Western modernism and addresses looting, colonial-era acquisitions and repatriation efforts.
Close

Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean
This course examines the painting, sculpture, and architecture of Renaissance Italy and the extensive artistic connections that linked the Italian peninsula to other regions of the world. By exploring a range of geographical contexts, from the Islamic courts of the Eastern Mediterranean and the commercial routes connecting Europe, Asia, and Africa to the newly encountered territories of the Americas, students will examine how trade, colonization, and cross-cultural exchange shaped the production and meaning of Renaissance art.
Close

Modern Art & Modern Museums
Examines debates on modern art through various themes. Focuses on the relationship between art and its presentation in museums and exhibitions, exploring curatorial practices and exhibition strategies.
Close

Writing Art's Histories
This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.
Close

Introduction to Literary Studies
Introduction to Literary Studies introduces practical criticism and literary interpretation. Students examine what literature is, why it is read and studied, formal properties and the constructed character of texts. Fiction, poetry and drama are supplemented by contemporary nonfiction and basic film narration, developing critical terms, tools and techniques.
Close

Film & Text
Studies complex links between literary and film narratives. Analyzes formal aspects of both media, discusses adaptation, intertextuality, viewer participation and narrative dynamics, and allows students to research topics like literature‑to‑film adaptation and cross‑cultural themes.
Close

Media & Race
Media & Race investigates storytelling, power, privilege, resistance and systemic racism in American history from the late nineteenth century to the present. Film, photographs, music and other media connect past and present. Students produce research-based podcasts exploring how media sustains oppression and supports resistance.
Close

The Documentary
Introduces documentary film from its early development to contemporary forms, analysing historical and social contexts, styles and genres, and ethical and aesthetic questions. Students analyse non-fiction representations and produce a short documentary item.
Close
